Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Scientists in Colombia have unearthed the remains of a true prehistoric monster believed to be the biggest snake ever to have lived on Earth. An artist's impression of what Titanoboa cerrejonensis would have looked like. Named Titanoboa cerrejonensis, the snake would have weighed 1,140 kilograms (2,500 pounds) and measured 13 meters (42.7 feet) nose to tail tip -- dwarfing the largest modern pythons and anacondas which can grow to 6 meters (19.5 feet). Scientists believe it slithered around the planet between 58 and 60 million years ago. Geologist David Polly, who identified the position of the fossil vertebrae which made a size estimate possible, said in a statement Wednesday: "At its greatest width, the snake would have come up to about your hips. The size is pretty amazing. "But our team went a step further and asked, how warm would the Earth have to be to support a body of this size?" Titanoboa's fossilized remains were discovered at a coal mine in the tropical Cerrejon region of northern Colombia by an international team of scientists. "Truly enormous snakes really spark people's imagination, but reality has exceeded the fantasies of Hollywood," paleontologist Jonathan Bloch, who co-led the expedition, told reporters. "The snake that tried to eat Jennifer Lopez in the movie 'Anaconda' was not as big as the one we found." Based on the snake's size, the team was able to calculate that the mean annual temperature in equatorial South America 60 million years ago would have been about 91 degrees Fahrenheit, about 10 degrees warmer than today, Bloch said. "Tropical ecosystems of South America were surprisingly different 60 million years ago," said Bloch. "It was a rainforest, like today, but it was even hotter and the cold-blooded reptiles were all substantially larger. "The result was, among other things, the largest snakes the world has ever seen...and hopefully ever will." According to Nature.com, snakes are poikilotherms (cold-blooded) that, unlike humans, need heat from their environment to power their metabolism. Therefore research suggests that at the time the region would have had to be no less than 86 to 93 degrees Fahrenheit for the snake to have survived. Most large snakes today live in the tropical regions of South America and south-east Asia, where the high temperatures allow them to grow to impressive sizes. Meanwhile, Carlos Jaramillo -- who was also part of the expedition -- said the tropical rainforest at Cerrejon appeared to have thrived at these temperatures. "This data challenges the view that tropical vegetation lives near its climatic optimum, and it has profound implications in understanding the effect of current global warming on tropical plants," he said.

# Giant prehistoric snake discovered in Colombia offers clues to a hotter ancient climate

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia** — Fossils unearthed in a vast Colombian coal mine revealed that the world’s largest known snake once slithered through the tropical forests of South America, offering scientists a dramatic glimpse into life — and climate — shortly after the extinction of the dinosaurs.

The species, named **Titanoboa cerrejonensis**, lived about **58 million to 60 million years ago** during the Paleocene epoch. Researchers announced the discovery in 2009 after studying vertebrae and other remains recovered from the Cerrejón coal mine in northern Colombia.

Scientists estimated Titanoboa reached about **42 feet (13 meters) in length** and weighed roughly **2,500 pounds (1,135 kilograms)**. Its massive body would have made it longer and considerably heavier than the largest anacondas and pythons alive today.

Titanoboa inhabited a hot, humid landscape of rivers, swamps and dense tropical rainforest. Fossils found alongside it — including giant turtles, crocodile-like reptiles, fish and abundant plant remains — suggest the snake was part of a rich freshwater ecosystem. Researchers believe it probably spent much of its time in or near water and may have hunted large aquatic animals.

The discovery also carried implications beyond the snake’s extraordinary size. Because snakes are cold-blooded and depend on external temperatures to regulate their bodies, researchers used Titanoboa’s dimensions to estimate how warm the tropics must have been.

The original analysis suggested that equatorial South America may have had average annual temperatures of roughly **86 to 93 degrees Fahrenheit (30 to 34 degrees Celsius)** — warmer than the region today. Such heat, scientists argued, would have provided enough energy for a snake to grow to Titanoboa’s enormous proportions.

That climate interpretation has since prompted scientific debate, with some researchers cautioning that body size can also be influenced by ecology, metabolism and evolutionary history. Still, Titanoboa remains important evidence that Paleocene tropical environments supported exceptionally large reptiles during a period when Earth had higher atmospheric carbon dioxide levels and little or no permanent polar ice.

The snake’s name combines “titan,” reflecting its immense size, with “boa,” its broader snake lineage. “Cerrejonensis” refers to the Cerrejón region where its fossils were found.

More than a record-breaking predator, Titanoboa has become a symbol of a dramatically different Earth — one in which steamy rainforests covered northern Colombia and a snake longer than a school bus dominated the waterways.

## Titanoboa: the giant snake from a lost rainforest

The snake most often described as the largest ever discovered is **_Titanoboa cerrejonensis_**, which lived about **58–60 million years ago**, shortly after the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs. Its fossils came from the **Cerrejón coal mine in northern Colombia**, where researchers were reconstructing one of the earliest known tropical-rainforest ecosystems.

The first remains—enormous vertebrae and ribs—were collected during expeditions beginning in the mid-2000s. Because snake skeletons are delicate and skulls rarely fossilize, the animal was initially reconstructed primarily by comparing its vertebrae with those of living boas. The species was formally described in *Nature* in 2009 by a team led by paleontologist **Jason Head**, working with **Jonathan Bloch**, **Carlos Jaramillo**, and others. Later expeditions recovered pieces of the skull, strengthening its identification as a giant boa relative.

### Just how big was it?

The original estimate put a large Titanoboa at roughly:

- **12.8–13 metres long**—about **42 feet**
- Around **1,100 kilograms**—roughly **2,500 pounds**
- Exceptionally thick-bodied, perhaps approaching **one metre across** at its widest point

Head emphasized how hard that scale was to visualize:

> “The snake’s body was so wide that if it was moving down the hall and decided to come into my office to eat me, it would literally have to squeeze through the door.”

Bloch offered a more cinematic comparison:

> “The snake that tried to eat Jennifer Lopez in the movie *Anaconda* is not as big as the one we found.”

Head likewise remarked:

> “Truly enormous snakes really spark people’s imagination, but reality has exceeded the fantasies of Hollywood.”

### Compared with modern anacondas and pythons

Titanoboa belonged to the broader boa lineage and probably resembled a greatly enlarged anaconda more than a python.

- **Green anaconda:** The heaviest living snake. Large, well-documented females are commonly around **5–6 metres**, with exceptional individuals reported beyond that, and may weigh **100–200 kilograms**. Titanoboa was therefore about twice as long as a very large, reliably measured anaconda and perhaps **five to ten times heavier**.
- **Reticulated python:** Generally considered the longest living snake. Exceptional verified specimens can approach **7 metres**, although many sensational claims of 9–10 metres are unsupported. Even the largest known pythons were far shorter and much lighter than the original Titanoboa reconstruction.

Like anacondas, Titanoboa probably spent much of its time in or near water. The Cerrejón environment was a hot, swampy rainforest inhabited by giant turtles, crocodile relatives and large fish. Its skull suggests it may have eaten fish as well as other sizeable vertebrates, rather than relying exclusively on constricting terrestrial prey.

### What it revealed about the Paleocene

The researchers initially used Titanoboa’s size to argue that equatorial South America must have been substantially warmer than today. Because snakes depend on external heat, they reasoned that an animal this large would have required average annual temperatures of approximately **30–34°C**. That climatic interpretation has since been debated: body size in snakes is influenced by ecology, food supply and physiology as well as temperature.

Titanoboa remains the **best-known contender for the largest snake in the fossil record**, though the title is not completely settled. In 2024, researchers described the Eocene Indian snake **_Vasuki indicus_**, estimating it at roughly **11–15 metres**. Because both genera are known from incomplete skeletons and their lengths must be extrapolated, it is not yet possible to say confidently whether Vasuki exceeded Titanoboa. Titanoboa nevertheless remains the iconic giant: a bus-length boa from the first great rainforests after the age of dinosaurs.

# Giant Prehistoric Snake Fossils Unearthed in Colombia’s Cerrejón Coal Mine

**CERREJÓN, Colombia —** Fossils recovered from one of the world’s largest open-pit coal mines have revealed the existence of *Titanoboa cerrejonensis*, a prehistoric snake estimated to have reached about **42.7 feet (13 meters) in length**—longer than a city bus and substantially larger than any living snake known to science.

The remains were discovered in the **Cerrejón coal mine in northern Colombia**, within rock layers dating to roughly **58 million to 60 million years ago**, during the Paleocene Epoch. That places *Titanoboa* only several million years after the mass extinction that ended the age of non-avian dinosaurs.

The discovery was formally described by an international research team in 2009. Rather than finding a single complete skeleton, paleontologists recovered numerous fossilized vertebrae and ribs belonging to several individuals. Researchers reconstructed the animal’s probable size by comparing its vertebrae with those of modern boas and anacondas.

Based on the largest known vertebrae, scientists estimated that the biggest individuals could have measured approximately **42.7 feet** and weighed around **1.1 metric tons**, although such figures remain reconstructions rather than direct measurements of a complete animal.

## A snake without a modern equal

*Titanoboa cerrejonensis*—its name meaning “titanic boa from Cerrejón”—was a member of the boid group, which includes today’s boas and anacondas. Its extraordinary dimensions surpassed those of the largest reliably measured living snakes.

Modern green anacondas are considerably shorter, though exceptionally heavy, while reticulated pythons can attain great lengths but do not approach *Titanoboa*’s estimated mass. The prehistoric snake’s thick body may have been close to a meter across at its widest point.

Researchers believe *Titanoboa* inhabited a hot, humid tropical environment of rivers, swamps and dense rainforest. Its massive body and the sediment in which its fossils were found suggest it may have spent considerable time in water, possibly living in a manner similar to a giant anaconda.

Exactly what it ate remains uncertain. Early portrayals often cast *Titanoboa* as a predator of crocodile-like reptiles, turtles and other large vertebrates. Later analysis of its skull suggested that it may have been particularly well adapted to eating fish. It could nevertheless have been an opportunistic predator capable of taking a range of aquatic and semiaquatic prey.

## Fossils emerge from coal-bearing rock

The Cerrejón mine has provided an unusually detailed view of life in the first major tropical rainforests to develop after the end-Cretaceous extinction. Coal extraction exposed extensive layers of Paleocene rock, giving scientists access to fossils that otherwise would have remained buried beneath northern Colombia.

Alongside *Titanoboa*, researchers have found giant turtles, fish and several kinds of crocodyliforms—reptiles related to modern crocodiles and alligators. Plant fossils show that the region supported a lush tropical forest with palms, legumes and other flowering plants.

The assemblage indicates a warm, water-rich ecosystem capable of supporting very large cold-blooded animals. It also shows that tropical ecosystems recovered relatively quickly after the extinction event 66 million years ago, which eliminated non-avian dinosaurs and many marine and terrestrial species.

Field crews working at Cerrejón initially collected large vertebrae that were not immediately recognized as belonging to a snake. Once specialists examined their anatomy, the scale of the discovery became clear. Individual vertebrae were far larger than those of living giant snakes.

## A clue to an ancient climate

Because snakes depend on environmental heat to regulate their body temperature, *Titanoboa* has also figured prominently in debates about Paleocene climate.

The research team that described the snake argued that an animal of its size would have required very warm tropical conditions. Initial calculations suggested average annual temperatures of roughly **30 to 34 degrees Celsius**, or **86 to 93 degrees Fahrenheit**, in equatorial South America.

That conclusion remains debated. The relationship between body size and climate in cold-blooded animals is complex, and factors such as behavior, access to water, metabolism and evolutionary history can affect how large an animal grows. Some researchers have cautioned against using *Titanoboa* as a simple “thermometer” for the ancient tropics.

Even with those uncertainties, the fossils support broader geological evidence that the Paleocene climate was warmer than today’s and that northern South America contained extensive humid forests.

## Reconstructing a lost giant

Scientists have recovered enough material to establish *Titanoboa* as the largest known snake in the fossil record, but many questions remain. No fully complete specimen has been found, and estimates of maximum length and weight depend on scaling relationships with living snakes.

A partial skull later helped refine ideas about its anatomy and feeding habits. Unlike many modern constrictors, *Titanoboa* appears to have possessed cranial features consistent with capturing large fish. Its sheer size, however, would have made it one of the dominant predators in its environment.

Paleontologists have not established whether it killed prey primarily by constriction, ambush, underwater capture or some combination of strategies. Popular reconstructions showing the snake battling crocodiles are plausible as dramatic illustrations, but they are not direct observations supported by preserved behavior.

## Lasting scientific importance

The importance of *Titanoboa* extends beyond its record-breaking dimensions. It provides evidence about how reptiles diversified after the disappearance of the dinosaurs, how quickly tropical forests developed during the Paleocene and how ancient climate influenced animal evolution.

The Cerrejón deposits also underscore the scientific value of industrial sites. Mining operations can expose fossil-bearing formations on a scale that would be difficult for researchers to excavate independently, although extracting fossils from active mines requires close coordination and rapid fieldwork before rock is removed or destroyed.

More than a decade after its scientific announcement, *Titanoboa* remains one of the most striking animals discovered from the Paleocene. Its fossils evoke a northern South America radically different from the region today: a hotter landscape of expansive wetlands, giant turtles and crocodile relatives, dominated by a snake that may have stretched nearly 43 feet from head to tail.

1. **Estimating body size from vertebrae.**  
   Titanoboa was known mainly from huge fossilized vertebrae found in Colombia’s Cerrejón Formation, about 58–60 million years old. Researchers compared the dimensions of these vertebrae—especially their width—with corresponding vertebrae from living boas and anacondas. Scaling those relationships upward suggested a snake roughly **13 meters long** and weighing around **one metric ton**.

2. **Linking snake size to climate.**  
   Snakes are ectotherms, so their body temperature and metabolism depend heavily on environmental heat. Among living snakes, the maximum body size found in a region generally increases with mean annual temperature: warmer climates allow very large snakes to maintain metabolism, digest food, and grow.

3. **Inferring ancient temperatures.**  
   Researchers plotted maximum snake size against temperature in modern tropical environments, then asked what temperature would be needed to support a snake as large as Titanoboa. The resulting estimate was a mean annual temperature of approximately **30–34°C (86–93°F)** in equatorial South America—several degrees warmer than many tropical regions today.

This was not a direct temperature measurement. It depended on assumptions that Titanoboa’s physiology resembled that of modern giant snakes and that temperature was the principal limit on its size. Later studies noted that behavior, food supply, evolutionary differences, and uncertain scaling could weaken the estimate, so Titanoboa provides evidence for an exceptionally warm Paleocene climate, but not a perfectly precise thermometer.

# Giant ancient snake discovery sheds light on tropical heat — and a warmer future

**By CNN Science**

Fossils unearthed in a Colombian coal mine revealed a snake so large that it challenges long-held assumptions about how tropical ecosystems function — and offers a striking glimpse of life in a much warmer world.

Named **Titanoboa cerrejonensis**, the prehistoric reptile lived about 58 million to 60 million years ago, several million years after the extinction of the dinosaurs. Researchers estimated that it grew to roughly 42 feet (13 meters) long and may have weighed more than a ton, making it the largest known snake.

The remains were discovered in the Cerrejón coal mine in northern Colombia, where scientists have also found fossils of giant turtles, crocodile relatives and some of the earliest known Neotropical rainforest plants.

“It’s a window into a lost tropical world,” said **Jonathan Bloch**, a vertebrate paleontologist at the Florida Museum of Natural History and one of the scientists who studied the site.

### A supersized tropical ecosystem

Titanoboa’s extraordinary size was not its only scientific significance. Because snakes are cold-blooded, or ectothermic, their body temperature and metabolism are strongly influenced by the surrounding climate.

By comparing Titanoboa’s vertebrae with those of living snakes, researchers reconstructed its size and used it to estimate the temperatures needed to sustain such a huge reptile. Their analysis suggested that equatorial South America was considerably warmer than it is today, with average annual temperatures possibly around 86 to 93 degrees Fahrenheit (30 to 34 degrees Celsius).

**David Polly**, a paleontologist at Indiana University who helped analyze the fossils, said the snake provided an unusual biological clue to ancient climate. A reptile of Titanoboa’s dimensions, the researchers argued, would have required consistently high tropical temperatures to maintain its metabolism.

That conclusion challenged the idea that tropical forests could not remain highly productive under extreme heat. The Cerrejón ecosystem appears to have supported abundant vegetation as well as enormous reptiles despite temperatures warmer than those in most modern rainforests.

Plant fossils studied by paleobotanist **Carlos Jaramillo** of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute showed that a diverse rainforest flourished there. The findings suggested that at least some ancient tropical ecosystems tolerated — and perhaps thrived under — levels of heat once considered too high for lush forests.

### Lessons for global warming

Titanoboa is not a simple model for what will happen as modern greenhouse gas emissions warm the planet. Its world differed greatly from today’s: atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were higher, continents and ocean circulation were different, and ecosystems had developed over long periods under those conditions.

Scientists have also debated how precisely the maximum size of ancient cold-blooded animals can be translated into temperature estimates. Factors such as food supply, habitat, evolution and physiology may also have helped Titanoboa reach its enormous proportions.

Still, the discovery carries an important message. Tropical ecosystems may respond to warming in ways that are more complicated than earlier models suggested. High temperatures do not necessarily mean the immediate disappearance of rainforests, but they can profoundly reshape which species dominate them.

Modern warming is also occurring far more rapidly than many ancient climate shifts, leaving plants and animals less time to migrate or adapt. Today’s forests face additional pressures from deforestation, fires and habitat fragmentation.

Titanoboa’s fossils therefore serve as both a scientific clue and a caution. They show that a hotter planet can support rich tropical life — but it may be a world populated by ecosystems unlike anything humans know today.
